Designing a way to hand out leads that nobody can argue with

Leadrat is a CRM real-estate brokerages run their sales pipeline on — from the moment a lead lands from a portal integration like MagicBricks to the moment an agent closes it. For an org running 30–100 agents against 100–500 inbound leads a day, the single highest-leverage decision in the whole system is the quiet one: which agent gets the next lead. I designed the configuration screen and the deficit-based algorithm behind it — a system that keeps every agent converging on their agreed share without ever needing to know how many leads are coming today.

00

The Question

How might we give admins flexible control over lead distribution — without making assignment complicated?

That is the question this case study answers. Everything below — the existing model, the shift in thinking, the system, the algorithm — is the working-through of it.

01

The Existing Model

Leadrat ingests leads from a stack of external portals — MagicBricks, 99acres, Housing, plus a brokerage's own site — into one CRM. Every account under Global Config gets its own lead-routing rules.

Before this project, opening that config for an integration meant landing on a bare list: which login was hooked up, whether the sync had completed, who the relationship manager was. There was no path from "here's an integration" to "here's how its leads get split across my team" — that logic didn't exist as a product surface yet. Two related requirements landed on my desk at once: a percentage-quota assignment algorithm, and a global configuration screen to drive it (and its round-robin sibling) from one place.

02

The existing model, in numbers

There was no configurable, weighted distribution logic anywhere in the product — leads went out ad hoc, or through a flat rotation that had no idea what an agent's real quota was supposed to be.

No weighting

A brokerage that had agreed 50/30/20 as a commission-driven split across three agents had no field anywhere to express that. Every agent got the same 1-in-N share, regardless of seniority, capacity, or specialization.

No live drift signal

An admin could not tell, mid-morning, whether an agent was ahead or behind their intended share — the only way to "check" was to manually count leads in a report at day's end.

Four disconnected paths

Assigning by user, by team, by project, and by property were four separate mental models with no shared screen, so an admin managing a multi-project brokerage repeated the same setup logic four times.

No accountability trail

When a quota changed, nothing recorded who changed it or when — a real problem the moment an agent disputes why their lead count dropped on a given day.

Scale for context: this is built for a mid-size deployment — roughly 30–100 agents against 100–500 inbound leads a day per org. At that volume, a percentage that's off by even a few points compounds into dozens of misrouted leads a week.

03

The Shift

The real shift was in the question itself: not “who gets this lead?” but “how should leads from this context be distributed?” Once assignment became a property of the context (a team, a project, a property) rather than a one-off decision, these were the questions that shaped the system:

01

How might we let an admin declare "50/30/20" as an actual enforced rule — without the system ever knowing how many leads will land today?

02

How might we still support teams that want plain round-robin fairness and nothing more sophisticated than that?

03

How might we fold four separate assignment targets — a person, a team, a project, a property — into one mental model instead of four settings screens?

04

How might we make every assignment, and every config change behind it, defensible after the fact?

04

The Algorithm: Deficit, Not Rounding

This turns out to be the same class of problem as apportioning parliamentary seats fairly across parties without knowing the final vote count in advance — the "largest remainder" family of methods. I adapted that logic to leads.

On every new lead, recompute what each agent should have by now, compare it to what they actually have, and hand the lead to whoever is furthest behind their own target. Nothing is pre-baked into a fixed rotation, so the system self-corrects continuously and works identically whether 3 leads or 3,000 arrive that day.

Expected(agent) = (Agent % / 100) × Total Leads So Far
Deficit(agent) = Expected(agent) − Actual(agent)
Next lead → agent with highest positive Deficit
Tie → agent with fewer total assignments so far
Run it yourself
Lead 0 of 12 — 50 / 30 / 20 split
Press Assign next lead to step through the exact worked example from the spec — Agent A opens with the first lead every time this split is used.
Straight from the acceptance criteria — Lead 5

Step through to lead 5 above and watch it happen: Agent A sits at 2 leads against an expected 2.5 (deficit +0.5), Agent B sits at 1 lead against an expected 1.5 (deficit +0.5) — an exact tie. The documented rule, "fewer total assignments wins," hands lead 5 to Agent B, not Agent A, because B has 1 prior assignment against A's 2. Across the full ten-lead example this is the only lead where the tie-break actually fires — which is why I treated it as a named, first-class rule in the spec (Decision 06 below) rather than an implementation footnote nobody would think to document.

Why not simpler options? A fixed repeating cycle (say, A A B A B C A B C) is cheap to build but can't survive an admin changing percentages mid-day — the cycle has no memory of what's already been paid out. Rounding each lead to the nearest integer bucket is the other obvious shortcut, and it breaks just as fast: at a 34/33/33 split, integer rounding starves the trailing agent for several leads in a row before it ever corrects. Recomputing the deficit on every single lead removes both failure modes at the cost of one lookup per lead — a trade I'd make every time at this volume.

05

The System, and the Screen It Became

The two requirements — percentage quotas, and a global assignment config — only make sense as one screen. Here's the reasoning behind the shape it ended up in, roughly in the order I made each call.

DECISION 01

Base before type

Alternatives considered
A single "assignment type" dropdown with percentage fields bolted on only for the percentage case; or two entirely separate screens per base.
Why this way
Sequential and Percentage aren't variations of the same form — they're two different philosophies of fairness. Asking "which philosophy?" first, then "assigned to what?", matches how an admin actually thinks about the decision.
Trade-off
One extra click for the simple round-robin case, every time.
DECISION 02

Four types, one shape

Alternatives considered
Keeping User / Team / Project / Property as four distinct flows, since each pulls from a different data source.
Why this way
All four resolve to the same thing underneath: a list of people. Giving them one shared "selected" panel — with a light contextual tag ("Aamor project") only where it adds information — let one screen replace four.
Trade-off
The panel has to visually adapt per type without becoming four screens hiding inside one.
DECISION 03

Running total, always visible

Alternatives considered
Validating the 100% rule only on Save, with an error toast after the fact.
Why this way
The requirement calls for real-time feedback, not a post-submit error — so the sum lives next to the inputs at all times, and Save stays disabled rather than allowing an invalid state to ever reach the assignment engine.
Trade-off
Disabling Save can read as "broken" to a first-time admin unless the gap to 100 is spelled out inline, not just implied.
DECISION 04

Additional Config as its own tab

Alternatives considered
Adding Real-Time Duplicates and Secondary Users as two more checkboxes on the main panel.
Why this way
Once duplicate-handling needed its own owner list, its own sequencing toggle, and its own selected-users view, it had the weight of a second decision, not a footnote to the first. Splitting it into a tab kept the primary panel scannable for the admin who doesn't need either option.
Trade-off
A feature an admin does want (duplicates) is now one tab away from where they land by default.
DECISION 05

"Same as Primary" defaulted on

Alternatives considered
Leaving Secondary Owners and Duplicate Owners as blank dropdowns an admin fills independently every time.
Why this way
In practice most orgs want the same person handling a duplicate as handles the primary lead. Defaulting "same as" to on turns the common case into zero extra clicks, while the checkbox stays there for the org that genuinely wants a separate duplicate-response team.
Trade-off
An admin who does need separate owners has to notice and uncheck a box that's on by default.
DECISION 06

Tie-break on assignment count, not randomness

Alternatives considered
The spec itself names two deterministic fallbacks — alphabetical order, or a round-robin cycle. Both are predictable; neither says anything about actual workload.
Why this way
Every assignment gets logged and can be questioned later, so I picked the tiebreaker that doubles as a fair answer, not just a consistent one. "Fewer total assignments so far" is provably correct in the spec's own example: at lead 5, A and B are both at a +0.5 deficit, and the rule hands it to B for sitting at 1 prior lead against A's 2 — an admin can explain that in one sentence, alphabetical order can't.
Trade-off
Slightly more state to track per agent (running totals, not just today's deficit) than alphabetical order would need.

What that produced, across every base × type combination:

turning this on had to reveal exactly one new decision — who handles the duplicate — not a second full config screen.

Real-Time Duplicates, switched on: a duplicate-owner list appears with the same "assign sequentially" option as the primary flow, so the mental model doesn't change, only the target does.

06

Guardrails

Input validation

0–100 only, numeric, no blanks. Errors surface inline as the admin types, not after they hit Save.

Save is a lock, not a warning

The Save button stays disabled until the total reads exactly 100 — an invalid split can't reach the assignment engine even for a second.

Immutable audit trail

Every save is timestamped and versioned, with who made the change. Nothing already logged can be edited or deleted — only added to.

Change isolation

Updating a quota mid-day only steers future leads. Leads already assigned before the change are never retroactively reshuffled.

07

Edge cases the spec forced me to design for

  • Low volume. The deficit math is continuous, not bucketed — the very first lead of the day always goes to the highest-percentage agent, which matches an admin's intuition even at n=1.
  • Simultaneous leads. Two leads landing in the same millisecond can't both read a stale "actual assigned" count — this pushed a real requirement back to engineering: atomic counter increments and row-level locking around the assignment write, not just the UI.
  • Concurrent config edits. Two admins editing the same account's quota at once needs the same locking discipline as the lead counters, or the audit trail records a change that was silently overwritten.
  • Permissions. Only roles with explicit rights can touch these settings — the config screen itself checks this before rendering editable fields, not just at the API layer.
08

Outcome

One outcome is provable without waiting for production data: run the exact 50/30/20 example from the spec through the simulator above, and by the tenth lead the split lands at 5/3/2 — a perfect match, no rounding drift, no manual correction. That was the acceptance bar engineering and I agreed on before writing a line of the interaction spec.

The rest is what I'd go measure on a live account before putting this in front of a hiring panel as fact rather than intent:

  • Change in manual reassignment tickets filed by admins, 30 days before vs. after rolloutEDIT
  • Average time to configure a new integration's assignment rules, before vs. afterEDIT
  • Agent-reported fairness (a short pulse survey) before vs. afterEDIT
  • Duplicate-leads-with-no-clear-owner, before vs. after Real-Time DuplicatesEDIT
09

Reflection

What I'd revisit

The tie-break rule is fair, but it's invisible — an agent has no way to see why they were skipped for a given lead. A lightweight "why this agent" trace, surfaced from the same audit log that already exists, feels like the next real iteration rather than a nice-to-have.

What I'd test next

Additional Config living behind a second tab was a deliberate bet that most admins configure duplicates second, not first. I'd want to watch a handful of first-time setups to confirm that bet rather than assume it from the requirements alone.

What this taught me

Designing the interface was the easy half. The harder, more interesting half was making a live mathematical guarantee legible — showing an admin, at a glance, that a system with no memory of "today's total" is still converging correctly.

Where I leaned on engineering

Concurrency (locking on the counters, isolation on config writes) isn't a UI decision, but it changes what the UI is allowed to promise. Getting that constraint early kept "immediate application" in the spec honest instead of aspirational.

10

My Role

  • Turned two written user stories and their acceptance criteria into one coherent interaction model instead of two disconnected screens.
  • Designed and checked the config panel across every assignment-base × assignment-type combination before handoff, rather than one happy path.
  • Worked with a backend engineer to pin down the deficit formula, the tie-break rule, and the concurrency behaviour it depends on.
  • Defined the audit-log data model — who, when, what changed — end to end, not just its list view.
  • Hand-ran the algorithm against the spec's own 10-lead example before dev handoff, to catch drift before a line of code existed.
  • Presented the decision log above to stakeholders and revised Decisions 03 and 05 after that review.
